explanations.explanation: Eighteen it is, friend. Luke says she had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years, hunched over and unable to stand up straight (Luke 13:11). That's a long, long time to carry that. I think eighteen years is worth slowing down for.

Twelve is close, but it's not this woman's number. Luke says she had been disabled by a spirit for eighteen years (Luke 13:11). That's six more years than twelve, and she was hunched over and unable to stand straight through all of them. I think eighteen is worth remembering.

Thirty-eight is a big number, but it's not this woman's number. Luke says she had been disabled for eighteen years (Luke 13:11). Eighteen years of being hunched over and unable to stand straight is already a long time. Eighteen is the number the text gives.

explanations.answer: He calls her over to Him
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. Luke says, "When Jesus saw her, He called her over…" (Luke 13:12). He saw her, and He called her over. No waiting, no committee meeting. I think being noticed like that meant a lot.

explanations.answer: He finishes teaching and finds her later
explanations.explanation: Nope, no waiting around on this one. The text says that when Jesus saw her, He called her over (Luke 13:12). It doesn't say He waited until later. He saw her, and she was called over right then.

explanations.answer: He sends His disciples to bring her outside
explanations.explanation: No middlemen here, friend. Luke says Jesus called her over Himself (Luke 13:12). No disciples sent, and no one is said to move her outside. She's called over right there in the synagogue, where He was teaching.
True! Jesus says, "Woman, you are set free from your disability." (Luke 13:12). Say it slowly, because eighteen years of bending came before those words. I think she heard every one of them.

It's actually true, friend. Jesus says to her, "Woman, you are set free from your disability." (Luke 13:12). Those are His words, right to her face. After eighteen years, I think those words landed like a gift.

Immediately! Luke says, "Then He placed His hands on her, and immediately she straightened up…" (Luke 13:13). No waiting room, no follow-up appointment. Eighteen years of bending, and it took no time at all once His hands were on her.

Not a night's wait, friend. The text says that after He placed His hands on her, "…immediately she straightened up…" (Luke 13:13). It didn't take until the next morning. It happened right then, in the synagogue.

A whole week? Not this time. Luke says "…immediately she straightened up…" once Jesus placed His hands on her (Luke 13:13). Seven days of waiting is a long haul, and she'd already done eighteen years. She didn't have to wait for one more.

She glorified God! Luke says she "…straightened up and began to glorify God." (Luke 13:13). First thing she does after eighteen years is give God the glory. I think that's the most beautiful thing she could have done with that first straight breath.

Tears wouldn't surprise me, but that's not what the text says. Luke says she "…straightened up and began to glorify God." (Luke 13:13). The Bible doesn't mention weeping here. What it does tell us is that she glorified God.

Home was probably calling, but Luke doesn't say she ran anywhere. He says she "…straightened up and began to glorify God." (Luke 13:13). She's still right there in the synagogue, standing tall and giving God the glory.

That's the one. Luke says the synagogue leader "…was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath." (Luke 13:14). A woman was set free, and the Sabbath is what he was upset about. I think I'd have been asking for a second look at my priorities.

explanations.answer: Jesus touched a woman in public
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text gives a different reason. Luke says the leader "…was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath." (Luke 13:14). The touch is not given as the reason for his indignation. The healing on the Sabbath is what bothered him.

Permission never comes up in the text. Luke says the synagogue leader "…was indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath." (Luke 13:14). It was the healing on the Sabbath that set him off, not the teaching.

Let's check the text, friend. Luke says the leader spoke to the crowd, saying, "There are six days for work… So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath." (Luke 13:14). He didn't go to Jesus. He said it to the crowd, so the answer is False.

False is right. The leader "…told the crowd." "There are six days for work… So come and be healed on those days and not on the Sabbath." (Luke 13:14). He spoke to the crowd, not to Jesus. The text doesn't say why he chose to speak to them.

explanations.answer: Unties it from the stall and leads it to water
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Jesus asks, "Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water?" (Luke 13:15). The ox or donkey gets untied and led to water on the Sabbath. I think Jesus was making His point with something they already did.

explanations.answer: Leaves it tied in the stall until evening
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Jesus describes. He asks, "Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water?" (Luke 13:15). Untied, not left tied up. They set the animal loose and led it to water.

explanations.answer: Brushes it down and lets it rest all day
explanations.explanation: A spa day for the donkey, I like it, but that's not the answer. Jesus says each of them would "…untie his ox or donkey from the stall and lead it to water?" (Luke 13:15). The animal gets untied and walked to drink, not brushed and left alone.

That's the synagogue leader's line, not Jesus'. The leader said to come be healed on the six days for work (Luke 13:14). Jesus says the opposite, asking, "Then should not this daughter of Abraham… be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?" (Luke 13:16). So the answer is False.

False, and you caught it. The leader was the one saying to come on the six days (Luke 13:14). Jesus asks, "Then should not this daughter of Abraham… be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?" (Luke 13:16). He's saying she should be released on the Sabbath day.
True. Jesus says Satan had kept her bound for "…eighteen long years…" (Luke 13:16). That's His own word for it, and He calls it her bondage. Then He says she should be released from it, and she was.

It's true, friend. Jesus says this daughter of Abraham was one "…whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years…" (Luke 13:16). Those are His words about what held her. He then asks if she shouldn't be released from that bondage.

Humiliated is right. Luke says, "…all His adversaries were humiliated." (Luke 13:17). That's what the text says happened to them after Jesus spoke. It's the opposite of what happened to the crowd, who rejoiced.
Rejoices, yes. Luke says, "…the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing." (Luke 13:17). The whole crowd, not just a few. They rejoiced at all the glorious things Jesus was doing.
Encouraged sounds friendly, but it's not the word. Luke says His adversaries "were humiliated." (Luke 13:17). Humiliated is what the text says. Encouraged is a good guess, but it isn't in the verse.

Grumbling would fit the synagogue leader's mood earlier, but not this verse. The crowd "…rejoiced at all the glorious things He was doing." (Luke 13:17). The word is rejoiced. The whole crowd was celebrating.

Trembling isn't in this verse. Luke says His adversaries "were humiliated," and the whole crowd "rejoiced" (Luke 13:17). Neither group is described as trembling. The text uses humiliated and rejoiced, so those are the words that fit.
